hints: Focus on what is actually getting hot here, it is the water that absorbs the heat, not the fuel that releases it.
Pick out your three numbers for q = mcΔT: mass of water is 200 g, c is 4.18 J g-1 °C-1, and ΔT = 75 - 25 = 50 °C.
Multiply them to get joules, then divide by 1000 to convert to kJ and see which option matches.
walkthrough:
**Identify what is being heated**

Think like this, the ethanol is just the heater. The water is what receives the energy, so we use the mass of water in our calculation.

$$m(\text{water}) = 200\ \text{g}, \quad \Delta T = 75 - 25 = 50\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$$

**Apply the heating equation**

For liquid water we use the specific heat capacity, the energy needed to warm 1 g by 1 °C.

$$q = mc\Delta T$$

**Calculate and convert to kJ**

Put the numbers in carefully, this gives joules first, then convert.

$$q = 200 \times 4.18 \times 50 = 41800\ \text{J} = 41.8\ \text{kJ}$$

**Ignore the distractor**

Notice the 2 g of ethanol tells you how the heat was supplied, but it is not needed to find the heat gained by the water. That is a classic Cambridge trap.

options.A: Uses the wrong mass. 2 x 4.18 x 50 = 418 J = 0.418 kJ uses the 2 g of ethanol instead of the 200 g of water. Always use the mass of the substance being heated, here the water.
options.B: Mixes up mass and temperature change. 50 x 4.18 x 50 = 10.4 kJ uses 50, the value of ΔT, as if it were the mass. Mass is 200 g, ΔT is 50 °C.
options.C: Correct. q = 200 g x 4.18 J g-1 °C-1 x 50 °C = 41800 J = 41.8 kJ. This is the heat absorbed by the water.
options.D: Uses the final temperature instead of the change. 200 x 4.18 x 75 = 62.7 kJ forgets to subtract the starting 25 °C. Heating is always driven by ΔT, not by T(final) alone.
